extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of constitutional theory, political philosophers, and policymakers interested in constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying normative criteria for what makes a sound constitution or form of government (e.g., mixed vs. simple governments, distribution of executive power, institutional limits). The page is a historical/political critique that lists standards and rules for preserving liberty and public safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of accusation
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberty of accusation must in some degree be admitted; without it neither will nor pleasure, nor law, can govern. It is 'essentially necessary for the preservation of a community' because persons must be held accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that unlimited liberty of accusation in a simple democracy would be disastrous (every member of a majority becoming informer/accuser). In a mixed government the liberty can be preserved equally to all without being excessive; the house will consider who is the accuser and the accused. Use institutional filters (grand inquests, juries, impeachments) to prevent abuse. Examples: Roman grand inquest and county inquests; historical dangers in simple governments and advantages in mixed constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of informers and calumny (private vs public motives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informers from private motives are justly odious; those from public motives are to be respected. Calumny itself is punishable as an offence against the public, and the injured individual may obtain satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions to distinguish public-spirited accusations from private, malicious ones. Mixed governments alone can manage calumny 'upon principles of public safety and private justice'—preventing hiding of crimes while punishing malicious slander. Historical examples and anti-patterns: prevalence of informers and calumniators under domineering elites; unchecked informer culture in simple democracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a mixed (three-branch) constitution with checks and balances
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixed government (e.g., English/American model) furnishes rules, means, and judicatures—grand and petit juries, impeachments—so that no crime can be concealed and laws maintain superiority; it produces constancy and security of life, liberty, honour, reputation, and property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that a constitution dividing power among legislative parts, executive, and judiciary creates mutual checks (king, senate, commons or similar) that restrain faction, balance rewards and punishments, and prevent tyranny of any one part. Use mixed institutions to ensure equitable administration of justice and to reduce the frequency of calumny, factional revenge, and unstable policy. Examples: contrasted with Rome (mixed elements) vs. simple governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject sole sovereign (single-assembly) constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A single sovereign assembly (one representative assembly with all power) exposes minorities and wealthy individuals to constant danger of false accusations and oppression; the majority would be omnipotent and parties would decide sentences more than truth or justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constitutions that concentrate legislative and executive authority in one assembly. Historical evidence and anti-pattern: in single assemblies every man's reputation, liberty, property, and life are 'in constant danger' of accusations by an omnipotent party; minority complaints are unheard. Prefer institutional separation to protect minorities and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit continuance of command and accumulation of offices (Non diurnare imperia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not permit the continuation of command and authority in the hands of particular persons or families; limit the duration of high offices (e.g., classical Roman practice limiting terms) to prevent the formation of a kingship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal limits on tenure (term limits, prohibition of successive terms) are necessary safeguards in simple democracies or aristocracies; in a well-mixed constitution continuance is less dangerous but still can be checked promptly if abuse appears. Examples: Roman censor term limits, Livy's warnings, the danger posed when elections are delayed and a man holds office beyond his term; Cincinnatus' resignation as exemplum. Anti-pattern: allowing life or prolonged command without effective checks invites monarchy/tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent particular persons from grandifying themselves (suppress aspiring-to-royalty behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not to suffer particular persons to greaten or to make themselves more than ordinary, because such ambition (affectatio regni) leads to aspirations to kingship and undermines liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should check personal ambition through laws and social sanctions (examples: Roman razing of Manlius' memory, caution about powerful families like Orange). Policies that allow or encourage the personal aggrandizement of military or political leaders are dangerous, especially in simple governments lacking countervailing powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewards and punishments governed by justice and sound policy, not by vague gratitude or jealousy
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice and sound policy should be the rule and measure of rewards and punishments rather than vague sensations of gratitude or jealousy; a balanced government is best able to ensure merit is rewarded and that injustice/ingratitude is minimized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design mechanisms to evaluate merit impartially (institutional vetting, balanced offices) so that real service is recognized while preventing royal favouritism or popular extravagance. Mixed governments reduce chances of ingratitude or injustice to deserving men and prevent excessive rewards for trivial services. Examples: contrasted ingratitude by princes vs. people's ingratitude; recommendation that 'justice and found policy' guide recompense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about educating youth in hatred of monarchy and binding abjuration oaths
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule 'to educate the young fry in principles of dislike and enmity against kingly government, and enter into an oath of abjuration' is criticized as iniquitous and dangerous—a device of aristocratical artifice that may lead to perjury or to creating worse evils (an unlimited monarchy) if circumstances change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should be wary of institutionalized indoctrination/oaths that permanently bar governance forms; such measures can backfire. Instead, foster balanced constitutional arrangements and avoid binding future generations to intolerant or impracticable oaths. Historical examples: Roman and Dutch abjurations; critique that such rules were inventions of aristocratical cunning and could force a people into perjury or extreme outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize social distinctions (gentlemen vs common people) and account for their political effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between 'gentlemen' (those with liberal education, influence, often richer) and the common people (labourers, mechanics, merchants); these classes have different capacities, interests, and tendencies to form parties and seek patrons, which produces division and risk of simple monarchy if unchecked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design must account for these social dynamics: the gentlemen's greater education and connections tend to concentrate influence, provoking resentment and faction among commoners; institutions should open paths to preferment for the common people and prevent capture of offices by narrow elites. Warning: policies that entirely remove gentlemen's share may provoke instability; balance is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of executive power affects patronage and class politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the common people place the whole executive power in one man, that executive will be forced to rely on and promote commoners to secure support—this can open roads to preferment for common people but also risks creating jealousies and ultimately concentrated power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of executive distribution must weigh trade-offs: single executive can democratize patronage and promotion, but risks enabling a strongman or monarchy if unbalanced; distributing executive responsibilities among branches reduces that risk and preserves rule of law. Historical/analytic guidance: consider how executive assignment shapes incentives for patronage and social alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy and universal vigilance of institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constituted government should produce constancy in its parts (king/branches/tribunes) and universal vigilance so that laws retain perpetual superiority and public tranquility arises from security under known laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitute overlapping, checking powers so that each branch is 'constant' to preserve its rights and to call back any branch that overreaches. This institutional constancy is the source of long-term security for life, liberty, property, and reputation. Use mutual accountability and regular, enforceable procedures rather than relying on rare exemplary characters.
